papers.title: Comparative outcomes of natural orifice specimen extraction surgery versus conventional minilaparotomy-assisted specimen extraction in colorectal cancer: A single-center retrospective study
papers.authors: Liao Y, Qiu R, Ma W
papers.abstract: Natural orifice specimen extraction surgery (NOSES) has emerged as an advanced minimally invasive technique that eliminates abdominal wall incisions for specimen retrieval; nevertheless, comparative data on its efficacy relative to conventional minilaparotomy-assisted extraction in colorectal cancer (CRC) remain limited. This retrospective analysis was conducted on 126 patients who underwent laparoscopic CRC resection at our institution, allocated to either the NOSES group (transanal specimen extraction, n = 49) or the conventional group (minilaparotomy-assisted extraction, n = 77), comparing perioperative parameters, postoperative recovery indicators, complication rates, and pathological outcomes. The NOSES group demonstrated significantly shorter time to first flatus (2.3 ± 0.9 vs 2.9 ± 1.1 days, P = .002), time to first liquid diet (3.1 ± 1.0 vs 3.8 ± 1.3 days, P = .001), and postoperative hospital stay (8.4 ± 3.2 vs 10.1 ± 4.1 days, P = .014). Visual analog scale pain scores on postoperative day 1 were significantly lower in the NOSES group (3.2 ± 1.1 vs 4.5 ± 1.3, P < .001), with reduced additional analgesic requirements (22.4% vs 44.2%, P = .014). Overall complication rates were significantly lower in the NOSES group (12.2% vs 24.7%, P = .043), with wound infections occurring exclusively in the conventional group (0% vs 6.5%, P = .045). No significant differences were observed in operative time, estimated blood loss, anastomotic leakage, lymph node yield, or R0 resection rate (all P > .05). In conclusion, NOSES appears to be a safe and feasible alternative to conventional minilaparotomy-assisted specimen extraction in highly selected patients with CRC, offering advantages in postoperative pain control, gastrointestinal function recovery, and wound-related complication reduction without compromising oncological integrity.

papers.title: The Hidden Conductor: HDL-Gut Microbiome Interplay in the Pathophysiology of Inflammatory-Based Diseases
papers.authors: Hafiane A, Kiss R, Favari E, Amedei A, Parolini C
papers.abstract: High-density lipoprotein (HDL) is a cholesterol transporter that plays a well-defined role in reverse cholesterol transport. In addition, HDL shows anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory functions mainly due to its ability to decrease the cholesterol content in lipid rafts, thus strongly influencing the membrane fluidity and the right localization/functionality of membrane-associated proteins (i.e., receptors/ligands) and their signal transduction pathways. Diverse experimental and clinical studies support the existence of a dynamic and complex relationship between HDL functionality and the gut microbiome (GM), with relevant implications for the pathophysiology of many widespread inflammatory-based diseases, such as cardiovascular disease (CVD), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), neurodegenerative disorders (NDDs) and cancer. Host factors (age, genes, dietary and lifestyle habits, medications) or environmental conditions may strongly negatively affect both the HDL system and the GM composition and function, promoting chronic low-grade inflammatory conditions that may exacerbate susceptibility to these human pathologies. Therefore, it can be hypothesized that the HDL-GM relationship may represent a novel therapeutic target to decrease the burden of these inflammatory-based pathologies. This review summarizes current data about the role of HDL and GM in the pathogenesis of CVD, IBD, NDDs and cancer, as well as findings that support the HDL-GM interplay as a crucial factor in the development of these relevant illnesses. Finally, we discuss the shortcomings of this relationship delineating the future directions to address them.

papers.title: Targeting the Microbiota-Metabolism-Immunity Axis: Active Components of Traditional Chinese Medicine in Colitis-Associated Colorectal Cancer
papers.authors: Chen Q, Zhang H, Fu L, Liu F, Yang Q, Zhang G
papers.abstract: Colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC) develops in the setting of long-standing intestinal inflammation and remains a major complication of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Although effective control of inflammation may reduce cancer risk, approaches that specifically prevent the progression from chronic colitis to neoplasia remain limited. Disruption of the gut microbiota-metabolism-immunity axis is increasingly implicated in this process, as microbial dysbiosis and altered metabolite production can compromise epithelial barrier integrity, sustain inflammatory signaling, and disturb mucosal immune homeostasis. This review examines how active components derived from traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), particularly flavonoids, alkaloids, saponins, and polysaccharides, influence this interconnected network in CAC-related models. Rather than treating these constituents as a single group, we compare the mechanistic patterns and evidence base associated with each class. Flavonoids and alkaloids have been studied mainly in relation to inflammatory signaling and epithelial barrier protection, whereas saponins are more often linked to regulation of the immune microenvironment. Polysaccharides have been studied most frequently in relation to microbiota remodeling, short-chain fatty acid production, and mucosal immune balance. These distinctions are not absolute, and substantial overlap exists across component classes. Moreover, most evidence is derived from animal or cell-based studies, with marked variation in experimental models, compound characterizations, dosing, and outcome assessments. The microbiota-metabolism-immunity axis provides a coherent framework for interpreting the multi-level actions of TCM-derived components, but their causal mechanisms and clinical relevance to human CAC require further validation.

papers.title: Viral-Gut Microbiota Interactions: Implications for the Gut Mucosa in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.authors: Wu Y, Hou L, Li Y, Li J, Hua X, He Y
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD), arises from complex interactions among genetic susceptibility, immune dysregulation, environmental factors, and the gut microbiome. Bacterial dysbiosis has been extensively studied, whereas the gut virome-comprising eukaryotic viruses and bacteriophages-remains less understood. Viruses can affect the intestinal barrier directly by infecting epithelial and immune cells, or indirectly by reshaping bacterial communities and host immunity. However, current evidence is dominated by cross-sectional associations and animal models, and whether virome alterations drive or result from intestinal inflammation remains unresolved. In this review, we provide a focused overview of intestinal barrier components relevant to IBD, synthesize human and animal evidence on IBD-associated viruses, and distinguish direct viral effects, microbiota-mediated effects, and bidirectional virus-microbiota interactions. We highlight bacteriophage-bacteria interactions as a central and potentially causal axis, discuss UC- and CD-specific differences, and outline causality gaps, search methodology, and emerging therapeutic strategies. Finally, we propose key unresolved questions and future research directions.

papers.title: Maternal-Fetal Exposome and Early-Life Microbiota-Pattern Recognition Receptors Signaling in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Susceptibility: A Mechanistic Review
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) develops through interactions among genetic susceptibility, intestinal microbiota, environmental exposures, and dysregulated mucosal immunity. Increasing evidence suggests that these interactions may begin before diagnosis-and possibly before birth-when maternal signals, microbial assembly, epithelial maturation, and immune education intersect. This narrative review synthesizes findings from human observational and cohort studies, experimental animal and cellular models, and mechanistic literature to examine how prenatal and early-life exposures may influence later IBD susceptibility. Human cohort studies associate later IBD with several early-life exposures, particularly repeated antibiotic use, whereas evidence for dietary, delivery, and household factors remains heterogeneous and vulnerable to confounding. Studies of pregnancies affected by IBD identify altered maternal and infant microbial and immune features but do not establish causality. Experimental models provide stronger mechanistic evidence that maternal microbial signals influence offspring immune development, neonatal epithelial cells acquire context-dependent tolerance, and microbial metabolites regulate regulatory T cells, type 17 immunity, barrier function, and chromatin-modifying enzymes. Histamine-receptor signaling further illustrates receptor-specific modulation of bacterial TLR (Toll-like receptors) responses in established IBD, although its role in early-life programming remains unproven. We propose a testable "developmental inflammatory set-point" model in which cell type, tissue compartment, timing, signal intensity, and host genotype determine whether microbial sensing promotes tolerance or persistent inflammatory readiness. This model is biologically plausible but remains unvalidated as a predictor of human IBD.

papers.title: Oral microbiome and inflammatory bowel disease: A scoping review
papers.authors: Chen C, Zhang H, Cheng T, Zhou F, Chen X, Fang M
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: To examine the association between the oral microbiome and IBD in terms of microbiota diversity, composition, function, and diagnostic potential through a scoping review of the existing literature.
METHODS: This scoping review was structured following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Literature searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, with the time frame restricted from database inception to November 17, 2025.
RESULTS: This review included 31 studies, among which seven topics for patients with periodontitis and IBD-related periodontitis, three studies assessed single bacterial species, and the remaining 21 articles explored the diversity and phylum-level taxonomic shifts of oral microbiota in IBD patients, functional and metabolic pathway alterations associated with oral dysbiosis, as well as the diagnostic potential and biomarkers derived from oral microbial profiles.
CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The oral microbiota of IBD patients exhibits characteristic dysbiosis, manifested by the enrichment of pathogenic taxa, depletion of anti-inflammatory species, and metabolic dysfunction, which are closely associated with gut microbial alterations and systemic inflammatory status. The salivary microbiome demonstrates significant diagnostic potential for IBD.
